In writing a prospectus for a frontier artificial intelligence IPO, you have to make choices about what to promise in your good vision of AI, and what to threaten in your bad vision. SpaceX went public this year promising “the largest actionable total addressable market (‘TAM’) in human history,” $28.5 trillion, which is a lot, sure, but still a finite number of dollars. OpenAI has raised money to build artificial general intelligence with the considerably more abstract promise that “it may be difficult to know what role money will play in a post-AGI world.” So the two benchmarks are something like “we will make more money than any company has ever made before” and “we will make money obsolete.” Anthropic is, by these standards, relatively sedate. From its founders’ letter: We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms. We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater. The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history. As one of the companies at the very center of that moment, we have a rare opportunity to shape it for the better. Our aim is to help humankind chart a safe course through this technological evolution, open new frontiers of discovery, and bring forth an age of miracles. Everyone who owns our stock, whether an institution or an individual, becomes part of that effort. We hope you will share our ambition to see it through. “Buy our stock for miracles” is pretty modest as AI hype goes. But it wouldn’t be an AI prospectus without threats. I searched in vain for words like “extinction” or “kill everyone,” but there are a couple of mentions of “existential risks to humanity.” The prospectus does not quite say “our products pose an existential risk to humanity.” It attributes that belief to someone else; it says that some people think Anthropic might pose an existential risk to humanity: Concerns have been raised both within our organization and by other researchers, regulators, policymakers, and industry participants that sufficiently advanced AI...

items.title: Money Stuff: Zuckerberg Wants to Keep His Votes
items.summary: Class C The basic deal is that if you found a company, and you want to raise money, you will probably have to give up some ownership of it. When the company is just you and an idea in your garage, you own the whole company. But if the company needs money to build factories or what have you, the people who give you the money will want something in return. Often what they will want is stock. If you hire employees, they will want stock. By the time your company is a big thriving public company, you might own only 10% or 20% of it. By that point, you might never again need to sell stock to raise money to do the company’s business. It’s thriving, it’s bringing in money, and if it is like the typical big US public company over the last few decades, particularly in the tech industry, it is bringing in more money than it needs to spend on growth. Until very recently , your company was more likely to be buying back stock than selling it. On the other hand, you might want money, for yourself. Maybe your yacht is getting a bit dingy, or you want to buy all the mansions around your mansion so no one can get too close to you. Probably you don’t have much liquid wealth other than the stock. So if you need a few hundred million dollars for yachts or mansions, the natural thing to do is to sell stock. But if you sell stock, you will own less of your company. You might, after founding the company and running it for many years and having your identity bound up with it, not like that. Well, tough. The thing that you have that has economic value is ownership of the company, and if you want to turn that into money you have to give up ownership. (Fine: You can borrow against your stock, which is not quite giving up ownership, though it creates some risk that you might have to.) There is a traditional compromise, which is that you give up some ownership but not control. Normally this is done with dual-class stock: Your shares get 10 votes per share, everyone else’s shares get 1 vote per share, so you end up with, perhaps, about 13% of the economic ownership of the company but about 60% of the votes. That way, you can pick the board of directors and run the company how you want, even while raising money — for yourself and for the company — from outside investors. If you sell some of your high-vote stock, it converts into low-vote stock, so you get money without giving up much control. You have to get your investors to agree to this, of course, and generally before you go public , but there is a long tradition of tech investors being fine with, and in fact liking , giving founders extra votes. items.title: Money Stuff: Obviously SpaceX and Tesla Will Merge
items.summary: SXSI/Tesla One model of Elon Musk five years ago is that he had a bunch of disparate interests and was really passionate about all of them. [1] One minute, he’d be like “I want to make self-driving electric cars,” and another minute he’d be like “actually I want to colonize Mars,” and then he’d be like “I want to teach a monkey to play Pong with telekinesis ,” and then he’d be like “actually I want to make Twitter more right-wing,” and then he’d be like “I don’t like traffic so, tunnels.” And he was enthusiastic and persuasive and had a good track record of succeeding with kooky-sounding ideas, so you’d be caught up in whatever crazy-sounding thing he was telling you. If you had a billion dollars and happened to talk to him about that day’s enthusiasm, you’d give him the billion dollars to do the thing. In some sense, the billion dollars was not for brain implants or tunnels or Twitter or whatever; you were giving him the billion dollars as a bet on him , as a bet that whatever weird thing he touched he could turn to gold. But in another sense, the tunnels mattered; his enthusiasm for specific weird projects was contagious. Perhaps you found tunnels boring [2] but were really excited about brain implants, so you gave him money for some projects but not others. I don’t know that this was the dominant model, though. More likely , on Monday you gave him a billion dollars for space rockets, and then on Wednesday he came back to you and was like “I need a billion dollars for tunnels,” and you were like “oh, right, of course, the previous billion dollars was for the rockets, I can see why you’d need a different pot of money for the tunnels.” In any case, by doing all the different projects in different companies with (possibly) different investors, he maximized his fundraising surface area. All of his investors got concentrated high-upside bets on whatever the relevant enthusiasm was. And then he went and did all of the things. There were some conflicts of interest involved in having one guy run all these companies doing all of these things. For one thing, there are only so many hours in a day, and if he’s spending 20 hours a day on Twitter he can’t spend 20 hours a day designing cars. Also, making Twitter right-wing might alienate a lot of electric-car buyers. But I don’t want to overstate this. These were very different things! A car company just does not compete with a space-rockets company, which does not compete with a brain implant company, which does not compete with a social media site. Oh there’s overlap; maybe the car company will borrow the rocket company’s rockets to make its cars fly. items.title: Against Against Handover
Money Stuff: Someone Has to Take the AI Risk
items.summary: AI CDS My basic model of the data-center stuff is that there’s a kajillion dollars of systematic data-center credit risk, and someone has to own it. Or in more words: Companies are borrowing a kajillion dollars to build data centers for artificial intelligence. The loans will get paid out of cash flows from renting the data centers to AI companies. Therefore, the loans will get paid back if AI companies have a kajillion dollars of revenue over the next few decades, and if they need all those chips in all those data centers to earn that revenue. [1] If AI revenue is lower than expected, if demand for chips is lower than expected, or if chips become obsolete faster than expected, that’s bad for the data-center loans. This risk is basically all systematic, not idiosyncratic. You might lend money to one particular data-center owner (a neocloud, a hyperscaler) that leases its data center to one particular AI-business tenant (an AI lab, a hyperscaler), and you might care about the underlying credit profile of the owner or the tenant, but it doesn’t matter so much as long as there’s a real data center filled with real AI chips. If AI takes off, revenue is high and chips are in demand, but your data center’s tenant falls behind and goes bankrupt, that’s fine: The owner will lease the data center to some other AI company and never miss a payment. If the data center’s owner goes bankrupt for its own idiosyncratic reasons, again, fine: These loans are largely property-level loans against the data center, and someone will buy the data center as long as data centers are in demand. [2] (If it goes bankrupt before building the data center , that’s maybe worse.) But there is systematic risk: If the market for data centers in 2032 is softer than expected, the data-center loans aren’t getting paid back. “Ah but my loan is backed by an investment grade hyperscaler so it will get paid back even if the AI boom is a bust,” you say , but really? All the investment-grade hyperscalers are betting a lot of money on the AI boom; in a bust scenario, are they all still investment grade? Therefore, investors will own a kajillion dollars of loans that either will all get paid off, if the AI boom goes as expected, or will all be in bad trouble, if not. Many of those investors — not, like, Leopold Aschenbrenner , but many of them — will want some sort of insurance against that giant systematic risk. “Hmm,” they think. “My whole portfolio has this big systematic bet on the AI boom . That is risky. I’d like to buy some insurance against the risk that it will go poorly.” Lots of people want lots of things, though. Who is going to sell them that insurance? items.title: Money Stuff: Universal Basic AI
items.summary: Public Benefit Fund The approximate rule for most US companies is: The company does stuff that generates economic value; Some of that value goes to the company’s workers as wages for creating the value; The company’s shareholders — founders and providers of equity capital, as well as employees who are paid in stock — share about 79% of what’s left; and Society gets the other 21%. That’s very loose. [1] But a company does some stuff, it makes some money, it pays some expenses, it has some extra money left over, which is called “income before income taxes.” And then 21% of that money goes to the US government as income taxes, and the other 79% stays at the company — and ultimately belongs to its shareholders — as net income. At a high level, this makes sense. The company benefits from society; roads and national defense and an educated workforce and a functioning legal system help create the conditions in which the company can make money. Society should get a cut of its profits. Why 21%? That’s just the law, just the headline US federal corporate income tax rate that applies to all companies. You could imagine things working differently. The other 79% — the portion of the company’s economic value that goes to its shareholders — is divided up differently at different companies, depending on those shareholders’ relative contributions and negotiating power. At some companies, most of the economic value goes to the founder; at others, to outside institutional shareholders. You could tell various stories about why that might make sense: Maybe some companies were bootstrapped and owe all of their success to their founders’ efforts, so the founders keep most of the value; other companies grew over time by deploying lots of outside capital and are run by hired professional managers, so the investors get most of the value. Or maybe it’s like “this company raised money from shareholders when valuations were high and terms were founder-friendly, so the founders kept most of the value.” You could imagine a similar variation in the 79/21 split. Like: “Some companies depend a lot on society, so they should pay more to society; other companies do not depend much on society, so they should not.” Or: “Society wants to encourage some companies and discourage others, so the discouraged ones have to give society more of their profits and the encouraged ones get to keep more.” Nobody quite puts it like that, but there really are a lot of credits and allowances and complications in the tax code, and many of them do gesture in the direction of encouraging stuff society — or at least Congress — wants and discouraging stuff it doesn’t. “Real estate developers are rugged individualists who owe nothing to society and create a lot of value for everybody else, so they should pay...

items.title: Money Stuff: Private Markets Are the New AI Markets
items.summary: Private beta Ten years ago I might have told a story like this. There are a bunch of companies in the world. As the economy grows, their profits will grow. If you buy their stocks, you will get a share of that growth. If you are a normal person saving for retirement, that’s a good thing to do: You want your savings to grow, and owning a share of growing corporate profits in a growing economy is a good way to do that. [1] The easiest way to do that is to just buy all the stocks in proportion to their market capitalizations, for instance in an index fund. Maybe you can do better than that: Maybe you can buy the companies that will grow a lot and avoid the companies that will go bankrupt. But that requires luck and skill and, crucially, it is zero-sum : If you buy the good companies and avoid the bad ones, that means someone else is buying the bad ones and avoiding the good ones, oops for them. Similarly, you could buy lottery tickets or day-trade stock options to get more than your share of economic growth. Same problem, though: Maybe you can get some extra return by winning the lottery, but that’s not a viable plan for everyone . Conventionally, owning a broad slice of the stock market gives you “beta”: It gives you exposure to the market return, which over the long term is mostly positive. Everything else — trying to beat the market by picking the right stocks or options or lottery tickets — gives you “alpha”: It gives you returns to skill, it gives you outperformance (or underperformance), it gives you something other than the broad market return. Beta is generally positive: Everyone can get rich owning the stock market. Alpha is generally zero-sum: Anyone’s outperformance requires someone else’s underperformance. There’s one other thing that doesn’t fit neatly into these categories. Some companies are not public; they don’t trade on the exchange, and their stocks do not contribute to the market return. Some companies are early-stage tech startups in someone’s garage; others were taken private in leveraged buyouts by private equity firms. Institutional investors can invest in those companies through private equity or venture capital funds. Is that alpha or beta? Some of both. It stands to reason that the smartest private investors would cherry-pick the best companies, help run them well, and get higher returns than the broad average of the public markets. But also, you know, these are companies, they participate in economic growth, the goal is for them to one day (re)join the public markets, and they will have some correlation to the public market return.
